title: Don't crowd them
hook: don't cramp people's homes or weary their lives (Tao Te Ching 72)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was knowing you don't know: being aware of where your knowing stops. Your line was I don't know.

A teenager's bedroom door, closed. On the other side, a parent with a question, a reminder and a worry, all lined up. Knock now, and the door may stay closed for a week. Wait an hour, and it might open on its own. Either side of that door is a hard place to stand. Chapter seventy-two of the Tao Te Ching is written to rulers, but it's about that hallway.
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR.` → `A QUESTION LINED UP.` → `KNOCK, OR WAIT?`

segments.voice: First, the warning. When people no longer fear what's fearsome, the chapter opens, something far more fearsome arrives. Pile on enough pressure and the pressure stops working, and what comes next is worse. Second, the instruction. Don't cramp the places where people live; don't weary the lives they lead. The old words are physical: don't press in on their dwellings, don't make them sick of living. Then a neat loop: only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you. Third, the sage's own room. The sage knows himself but doesn't put himself on show, and cares for himself but doesn't set himself up high. Someone who doesn't need to be seen, or to be above, has less reason to crowd anyone else. Fourth, the week, which ends here. Rivers and seas lead because they lie lower. Three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward. Coarse cloth with jade inside. Knowing you don't know. Today fits the run: they're all ways of taking up less space so others have more. Room looks like a question asked once instead of three times, a plan left open for someone else to fill, not reading over a shoulder.
screen: `PRESSURE STOPS WORKING.` · `DON'T CRAMP THEIR HOMES.` · `NO NEED TO BE SEEN.` · `A WEEK OF TAKING LESS SPACE.` · then, large: `GIVE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Let your breath find its own pace, giving it room too, and bring to mind one person you've been pressing on, even gently: a child, a partner, a coworker, a friend who owes you a reply. Picture the space around them, and ask what you could stop asking, checking or reminding, just for today. Rest with the space that leaves.
Don't crowd them. Chapter seventy-two: don't cramp where people live or weary the lives they lead; if you don't weary them, they won't weary of you. Today's word.
Your line: give room. Less pressure leaves more space for them to come to you. Until next time.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-two as advice on governing and on any kind of authority: don't press in on people's homes or lives, and they won't turn against you.

notes: Week-end day: looks back at days 1128–1133; the editor checked the recap against those scripts.
The three treasures are named here as gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first, matching day 1129's Legge wording (chapter 67).
Chapter 72 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording. The opening line 民不畏威，則大威至 is read here as a warning about pressure backfiring; some read 威 differently. Confirm.
Trapdoor: 厭 (yàn) is used twice in 夫唯不厭，是以不厭; confirm.
Original 無狎其所居 (wú xiá qí suǒ jū) rendered 'woo SHYAH chee swaw JYOO'. Some editions read 狹 for 狎. Confirm.
Editor: the three treasures now use day 1129's wording (gentleness, economy) instead of kindness, frugality; the practice no longer repeats day 1131's stepping-back image.
